claim: The coordinated motion of animal groups through fluids is thought to reduce the cost of locomotion to individuals in the group.
source: The coordinated motion of animal groups through fluids is thought to reduce the cost of locomotion to individuals in the group.
evidence: This is a general statement about the hypothesis that group movement reduces locomotion costs, supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: In side-by-side arrangements, the reciprocal nature of flow coupling results in an equal distribution of energy requirements among all members.
source: in side-by-side arrangements, the reciprocal nature of flow coupling results in an equal distribution of energy requirements among all members
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 7C.

claim: Swimmers flapping inphase in side-by-side arrangements experience a reduction in cost of locomotion.
source: with reduction in cost of locomotion for swimmers flapping inphase
evidence: This is supported by computational results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Swimmers flapping antiphase in side-by-side arrangements experience an increase in cost of locomotion.
source: but an increase in cost for swimmers flapping antiphase
evidence: This is supported by computational results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In inline arrangements, flow coupling is non-reciprocal for all flapping phase.
source: in inline arrangements, flow coupling is non-reciprocal for all flapping phase
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B and discussed in the Results section.

claim: In inline arrangements, energetic savings favor trailing swimmers.
source: with energetic savings in favor of trailing swimmers
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A and Figure 7C showing that followers receive hydrodynamic benefits while leaders do not.

claim: Inline arrangements maintain energetic benefits only up to a finite number of swimmers.
source: but only up to a finite number of swimmers, beyond which school cohesion and energetic benefits are lost at once
evidence: This is supported by simulation data in Figures 7 and 8 showing that inline formations split when the number of swimmers exceeds a critical value.

claim: Direct energetic measurements in moving animals are notoriously difficult and often unreliable as proxy for hydrodynamic energy savings.
source: because direct energetic measurements in moving animals, flying or swimming, are notoriously difficult and often unreliable as proxy for hydrodynamic energy savings (Herskin and Steffensen, 1998; Killen et al., 2012; Marras et al., 2015; Li et al., 2020; Zhang and Lauder, 2023a; Thandiackal and Lauder, 2023; Zhang and Lauder, 2023b; Marras and Porfiri, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to existing literature.

claim: Animal groups do not generally conform to regular patterns and individuals dynamically change their position relative to their neighbors.
source: chiefly because animal groups do not generally conform to regular patterns – individuals in these groups dynamically change their position relative to their neighbors (Partridge and Pitcher, 1979; Svendsen et al., 2003; Marras et al., 2015; Ashraf et al., 2017; Mirzaeinia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental observations in the literature.

claim: Li et al., 2020, associated energy savings in pairs of flapping robotic swimmers with a linear relationship between their flapping phase lag and relative distance.
source: Li et al., 2020, associated energy savings in pairs of flapping robotic swimmers with a linear relationship between their flapping phase lag and relative distance.
evidence: This is a direct reference to findings from Li et al., 2020.

claim: The linear phase-distance relationship was uncovered independently in flapping hydrofoils and accredited solely to flow interactions.
source: Interestingly, the same linear phase-distance relationship was uncovered independently in flapping hydrofoils and accredited solely to flow interactions (Zhu et al., 2014; Newbolt et al., 2019; Newbolt et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on flapping hydrofoils.

claim: Zhang and Lauder, 2023b, reported impressive energetic savings attributed to schooling compared to solitary swimming when fish were challenged to swim at high speeds.
source: metabolic energetic measurements were recently performed in solitary and groups of eight fish, and impressive energetic savings were attributed to schooling compared to solitary swimming when the fish were challenged to swim at high speeds (Zhang and Lauder, 2023b).
evidence: This is a direct reference to experimental findings from Zhang and Lauder, 2023b.

claim: The study by Zhang and Lauder, 2023b, made no mention of the spatial patterns assumed by the fish.
source: Lamentably, the study made no mention of the spatial patterns assumed by these physically thwarted individuals (Zhang and Lauder, 2023b).
evidence: This is a critical observation about what was not reported in Zhang and Lauder, 2023b.

claim: Ashraf et al., 2017, showed that when challenged to sustain higher swimming speeds, fish in a group rearranged themselves in a side-by-side pattern as the speed increased.
source: Specifically, Ashraf et al., 2017, showed that, when challenged to sustain higher swimming speeds, the fish in a group rearranged themselves in a side-by-side pattern as the speed increased, presumably to save energy.
evidence: This is a direct reference to experimental observations from Ashraf et al., 2017.

claim: Marras et al., 2015, reported that side-by-side formations, though beneficial, produce the least energetic savings compared to diagonal formations.
source: The metabolic measurements of Marras et al., 2015, in a school of eight fish report that side-by-side formations, though beneficial, produce the least energetic savings compared to diagonal formations (Weihs, 1973).
evidence: This is a direct reference to experimental findings from Marras et al., 2015.

claim: In an experimental study of a single fish interacting with a robotic flapping foil, the freely swimming fish positioned itself in an inline formation in the wake of the flapping foil.
source: In an experimental study of a single fish interacting with a robotic flapping foil, the freely swimming fish positioned itself in an inline formation in the wake of the flapping foil, supporting the hypothesis that swimming in the wake of one another is an advantageous strategy to save energy in a school (Thandiackal and Lauder, 2023).
evidence: This is a direct reference to experimental observations from Thandiackal and Lauder, 2023.

claim: Side-by-side formations where fish mirror each other by flapping antiphase are thought to create a wall-like effect that reduces swimming cost.
source: For example, side-by-side formations, where fish mirror each other by flapping antiphase, are thought to create a wall-like effect that reduces swimming cost (Zhang and Lauder, 2023b; Fish and Hui, 1991).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature about the mechanism of energy savings in side-by-side antiphase formations.

claim: A fish swimming in the wake between two leading fish encounters a reduced oncoming velocity, leading to reduced drag and thrust production.
source: A fish swimming in the wake between two leading fish encounters a reduced oncoming velocity, leading to reduced drag and thrust production (Weihs, 1973).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Weihs, 1973, about the mechanism of energy savings in certain formations.

claim: Inline formations where fish swim in tandem are thought to provide benefits to both leader and follower by an added mass push from follower to leader and a reduced pressure on the follower.
source: Inline formations, where fish swim in tandem, are thought to provide benefits to both leader and follower, by an added mass push from follower to leader (Fish and Hui, 1991; Usherwood et al., 2011) and a reduced pressure on the follower (Kurt and Moored, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature about the mechanism of energy savings in inline formations.

claim: A single flapping hydrofoil shares many hydrodynamic aspects with its biological counterpart, including an alternating, long-lived pattern of vorticity in its wake.
source: Namely, we represent each fish as a freely swimming hydrofoil undergoing pitching oscillations about its leading edge. A single flapping hydrofoil shares many hydrodynamic aspects with its biological counterpart, including an alternating, long-lived pattern of vorticity in its wake (Triantafyllou et al., 1993; Triantafyllou et al., 2000; Lauder et al., 2011; Verma et al., 2017; Smits, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating similarities between flapping hydrofoils and swimming fish.

claim: Flow interactions with no sensing and feedback control lead to emergent formations that preserve the linear phase-distance relationship uncovered in live and robotic fish and in flapping hydrofoils.
source: In this study, we show, based on our own simulations and by conducting a thorough literature survey, that flow interactions, with no sensing and feedback control, lead to emergent formations that preserve the linear phase-distance relationship uncovered independently in live and robotic fish (Li et al., 2020; Thandiackal and Lauder, 2023) and in flapping hydrofoils (Zhu et al., 2014; Newbolt et al., 2019; Newbolt et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' simulations and literature review, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The linear phase-distance relationship is preserved irrespective of geometry, material properties, and flapping kinematics.
source: This relationship is preserved irrespective of geometry (Ramananarivo et al., 2016; Newbolt et al., 2019; Newbolt et al., 2022), material properties (Kim et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2014; Peng et al., 2018; Arranz et al., 2022), and flapping kinematics (Heydari and Kanso, 2021; Kurt et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing the universality of the linear phase-distance relationship.

claim: Inline formations differentially distribute hydrodynamic savings to members within the school, favoring trailing swimmers, but only up to a certain school size.
source: Importantly, we go beyond two swimmers to investigate flow interactions in larger groups and find that inline formations differentially distribute hydrodynamic savings to members within the school, favoring trailing swimmers, but only up to a certain school size
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Side-by-side formations equally distribute hydrodynamic savings and scale to arbitrary number of swimmers without loss of cohesion.
source: while side-by-side formations equally distribute hydrodynamic savings and scale to arbitrary number of swimmers without loss of cohesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pairs of flapping swimmers self-organize into inline, diagonal, or side-by-side formations.
source: We found that a pair of flapping swimmers self-organize into inline, diagonal, or side-by-side formations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: A perfect side-by-side configuration of inphase flapping swimmers is unstable.
source: That is, a perfect side-by-side configuration of inphase flapping swimmers is unstable but the more commonly observed configuration (Li et al., 2020) where the two swimmers are slightly shifted relative to each other is stable.
evidence: This is inferred from simulation results and is consistent with observations in Li et al., 2020.

claim: Both side-by-side equilibria (inphase and antiphase) were observed experimentally in heaving hydrofoils.
source: Both side-by-side equilibria were observed experimentally in heaving hydrofoils (Newbolt et al., 2022), albeit with no assessment of the associated hydrodynamic power and cost of transport.
evidence: This is a reference to experimental observations from Newbolt et al., 2022.

claim: Pairs of flapping swimmers passively self-organize into equilibrium formations independent of both scale and fluid model.
source: The key observation, that pairs of flapping swimmers passively self-organize into equilibrium formations, is independent of both scale and fluid model.
evidence: This is supported by simulations at different Reynolds numbers and dissipation times shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The fact that equilibria emerge in time-forward simulations is indicative of stability.
source: The fact that these equilibria emerge in time-forward simulations is indicative of stability (Strogatz, 1994).
evidence: This is a general principle from dynamical systems theory.

claim: In all cases except for the antiphase side-by-side formation, swimmers traveling in equilibrium formations save power and cost of transport compared to solitary swimming.
source: In all cases, except for the antiphase side-by-side formation, in both CFD and VS simulations, the swimmers traveling in equilibrium formations save power and cost of transport compared to solitary swimming.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For inline and diagonal formations, hydrodynamic benefits are granted entirely to the follower, whose hydrodynamic savings can be as high as 60% compared to solitary swimming.
source: For inline and diagonal formations, these hydrodynamic benefits are granted entirely to the follower, whose hydrodynamic savings can be as high as 60% compared to solitary swimming (Figure 3A; Heydari and Kanso, 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with Heydari and Kanso, 2021.

claim: Flow coupling between two inline or diagonal swimmers is non-reciprocal because the follower positioned in or close to the leader's wake interacts more strongly with that wake than the leader interaction with the follower's wake.
source: Intuitively, because in 2D flows, vortex-induced forces decay with the inverse of the square of the distance from the vortex location, flow coupling between the two inline or diagonal swimmers is non-reciprocal; the follower positioned in or close to the leader's wake interacts more strongly with that wake than the leader interaction with the follower's wake (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A, B and 4A, B).
evidence: This is explained by the physics of 2D flows and is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: In side-by-side formations, by symmetry, flow coupling between the two swimmers is reciprocal, or nearly reciprocal in inphase flapping.
source: In side-by-side formations, by symmetry, flow coupling between the two swimmers is reciprocal, or nearly reciprocal in inphase flapping (Figure 1—figure supplements 1C, D and 4C, D).
evidence: This is explained by symmetry arguments and is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: For inphase flapping in side-by-side formations, the hydrodynamic benefits are shared equally between both swimmers.
source: Indeed, for inphase flapping, the hydrodynamic benefits are shared equally between both swimmers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For antiphase flapping in side-by-side formations, the cost is also shared equally.
source: For antiphase flapping the cost is also shared equally (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Flow-coupled flapping swimmers passively organize into stable traveling equilibrium formations with linear phase-distance relationship independent of geometric layout, flapping kinematics, material properties, tank geometry, fidelity of the fluid model, and system.
source: These findings strongly indicate that flow-coupled flapping swimmers passively organize into stable traveling equilibrium formations with linear phase-distance relationship. This relationship is independent of the geometric layout (inline versus laterally offset swimmers), flapping kinematics (heaving versus pitching), material properties (rigid versus flexible), tank geometry (rotational versus translational), fidelity of the fluid model (CFD versus VS versus particle model), and system (biological versus robotic, 2D versus 3D).
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from the authors' simulations and literature review.

claim: Vortex phase matching is an outcome of passive flow interactions among flapping swimmers, and not necessarily an active strategy implemented by fish via sensing and feedback mechanisms.
source: However, they proffer that vortex phase matching is an outcome of passive flow interactions among flapping swimmers, and not necessarily an active strategy implemented by fish via sensing and feedback mechanisms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Emergent side-by-side formations can be predicted from symmetry arguments.
source: Second, they led us to hypothesize that emergent side-by-side formations can be predicted from symmetry arguments
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Emergent inline and diagonal formations can be predicted entirely from kinematic considerations of the leader's wake without considering two-way flow coupling between the two swimmers.
source: while emergent inline and diagonal formations can be predicted entirely from kinematic considerations of the leader's wake without considering two-way flow coupling between the two swimmers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and tested in subsequent sections.

claim: Locations of maximum flow agreement parameter V(x,y;ϕ) closely coincide with the stable equilibria obtained from solving pairwise interactions.
source: In both CFD and VS simulations, the locations with the maximum flow agreement parameter closely coincide with the stable equilibria (black circles) obtained from solving pairwise interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the flow agreement parameter field with actual equilibria in Figure 4.

claim: Hydrodynamic coupling in pairs of flapping swimmers is primarily non-reciprocal – captured solely by consideration of the effects of the leader's wake on the follower.
source: These findings imply that hydrodynamic coupling in pairs of flapping swimmers is primarily non-reciprocal – captured solely by consideration of the effects of the leader's wake on the follower.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that the leader's wake alone can predict equilibria.

claim: Predictions of the equilibrium configurations based on maximal flow agreement parameter agree remarkably well with actual equilibria based on pairwise interactions.
source: Predictions of the equilibrium configurations based on maximal flow agreement parameter agree remarkably well with actual equilibria based on pairwise interactions, and they all follow the universal linear phase-distance relationship shown in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Larger values of the flow agreement parameter V imply more power savings and reduced cost of transport.
source: Assessment of the relative power savings follows directly from the maximal value of the flow agreement parameter: larger values imply more power savings and reduced cost of transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Swimmers can take great liberty in changing their phase without compromising much the average energy savings of the school, as long as they maintain close lateral distance to their neighbor.
source: That is, swimmers can take great liberty in changing their phase without compromising much the average energy savings of the school, as long as they maintain close lateral distance to their neighbor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the parametric study results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In each subgroup of inline swimmers, swimmer 3 experiences the largest hydrodynamic advantage (up to 120% power saving), swimmer 2 receives benefits comparable to those it received in pairwise formation (65% power saving), and swimmer 1 no benefit at all.
source: In each subgroup, swimmer 3 experiences the largest hydrodynamic advantage (up to 120% power saving!), swimmer 2 receives benefits comparable to those it received in pairwise formation (65% power saving), and swimmer 1 no benefit at all (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power savings data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In a school of three inline swimmers, flow interactions led to a stable emergent formation with hydrodynamic benefits similar to those experienced by the three swimmers in each subgroup of a six-swimmer school.
source: We found that in a school of three inline swimmers, flow interactions led to a stable emergent formation with hydrodynamic benefits similar to those experienced by the three swimmers in each subgroup of Figure 7A and C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: When computing the motion of four inline swimmers, the leading three swimmers maintained cohesion, but swimmer 4 separated and lagged behind, receiving no advantage in terms of power savings.
source: When computing the motion of four inline swimmers (Figure 8A), we found that the leading three swimmers maintained cohesion, at hydrodynamic benefits similar to a formation of three, but swimmer 4 separated and lagged behind, receiving no advantage in terms of power savings because it split from the formation (Figure 8D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 8A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In a group of five inline swimmers, the last two swimmers split and formed their own subgroup.
source: In a group of five, the last two swimmers split and formed their own subgroup.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all examples of inline formations, swimmer 4 consistently lost hydrodynamic advantage and served as local leader of the trailing subgroup.
source: That is, in all examples, swimmer 4 consistently lost hydrodynamic advantage and served as local leader of the trailing subgroup.
evidence: This is an observation from simulation results shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Flow interactions alone are insufficient to maintain inline formations as the group size increases.
source: These observations are consistent with Peng et al., 2018, and demonstrate that flow interactions alone are insufficient to maintain inline formations as the group size increases.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results and is consistent with Peng et al., 2018.

claim: Swimmers in side-by-side formations reached stable configurations reminiscent of the configurations observed experimentally when fish were challenged to swim at higher swimming speeds.
source: The swimmers reached stable side-by-side formations reminiscent of the configurations observed experimentally when fish were challenged to swim at higher swimming speeds (Ashraf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7B and is consistent with Ashraf et al., 2017.

claim: Swimmers in side-by-side configurations saved power compared to solitary swimming: swimmers gained equally in terms of hydrodynamic advantage (up to 55% power saving for the middle swimmers in a school of six), except the two edge swimmers which benefited less.
source: The swimmers in this configuration saved power compared to solitary swimming (Figure 7C): swimmers gained equally in terms of hydrodynamic advantage (up to 55% power saving for the middle swimmers in a school of six), except the two edge swimmers which benefited less.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power savings data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The robustness and overall trend of power saving among group members is robust to the total number of swimmers in side-by-side formations.
source: The robustness and overall trend of power saving among group members is robust to the total number of swimmers in these side-by-side formations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the wake of a two-swimmer school, positive flow agreement in the region is enlarged and enhanced, corresponding to swimmer 3 receiving the largest power savings.
source: Compared to the single leader wake in Figure 4B, in the wake of a two-swimmer school, positive flow agreement in the (blue) region is enlarged and enhanced, corresponding to swimmer 3 receiving the largest power savings.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flow agreement parameter field shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Behind three inline swimmers, the region of positive flow agreement is weakened and shrunk, indicating weaker potential for energy saving by a fourth swimmer.
source: On the other hand, behind three inline swimmers, the region of positive flow agreement is weakened and shrunk, indicating weaker potential for energy saving by a fourth swimmer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the flow agreement parameter field shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The number of swimmers that passively maintain a cohesive inline formation is not a universal property of the flow physics, but depends on the flow regime.
source: We thus hypothesized that the number of swimmers that passively maintain a cohesive inline formation is not a universal property of the flow physics, but depends on the flow regime.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: In CFD simulations at Re=1645, an inline school of three swimmers remains cohesive, but a fourth swimmer collides with the upstream swimmer.
source: We additionally tested the stability of inline formations in CFD simulations at Re=1645 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and observed the same trend: an inline school of three swimmers remains cohesive, but a fourth swimmer collides with the upstream swimmer.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFD simulation results shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of cohesion in inline formations does not depend on the specific fluid model.
source: These observations imply that the loss of cohesion does not depend on the specific fluid model.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in both CFD and VS models.

claim: In Peng et al., 2018, the authors employed flexible heaving foils at Re = 200 and observed stable inline formations with larger number of swimmers.
source: This is consistent qualitatively with existing results (Peng et al., 2018). In Peng et al., 2018, the authors employed flexible heaving foils at Re = 200 and observed stable inline formations with larger number of swimmers.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from Peng et al., 2018.

claim: The flexible foil model and smaller Re make the swimmer more adaptive to changes in the flow field, by passively modulating the amplitude and phase along its body, thus diverting some of the hydrodynamic energy into elastic energy and stabilizing the larger inline formation.
source: The flexible foil model and smaller Re make the swimmer more adaptive to changes in the flow field, by passively modulating the amplitude and phase along its body, thus diverting some of the hydrodynamic energy into elastic energy and stabilizing the larger inline formation.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observations in Peng et al., 2018.

claim: The number of swimmers in a stable inline group is not a universal property of the formation, rather it is model and scale-dependent.
source: This, again, emphasizes that the number of swimmers in a stable inline group is not a universal property of the formation, rather it is model and scale-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' findings and comparison with Peng et al., 2018.

claim: When phase control was applied to swimmer 4 in a school of four inline swimmers, it led to a stable formation, albeit at no benefit to swimmer 4; in fact, swimmer 4 spent 100% more power compared to solitary swimming.
source: When applied to swimmer 4 (Figure 10A), this phase controller led to a stable formation, albeit at no benefit to swimmer 4; in fact, swimmer 4 spent 100% more power compared to solitary swimming
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The power savings of swimmers 2 and 3 remained robustly at the same values as in the formation without swimmer 4 when phase control was applied to swimmer 4.
source: whereas the power savings of swimmers 2 and 3 remained robustly at the same values as in the formation without swimmer 4.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 10A.

claim: By the non-reciprocal nature of flow interactions, changing the phase of the trailing swimmer has little effect on the oncoming flow field generated by the upstream swimmers.
source: The inability of swimmer 4 to extract hydrodynamic benefits from the oncoming flow is due to a fundamental physical limitations, as explained in Figure 9; by the non-reciprocal nature of flow interactions, changing the phase of the trailing swimmer has little effect on the oncoming flow field generated by the upstream swimmers.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the non-reciprocal nature of flow coupling.

claim: If the oncoming wake itself presents no opportunity for hydrodynamic benefit, phase control cannot generate such benefit.
source: If the oncoming wake itself presents no opportunity for hydrodynamic benefit, phase control cannot generate such benefit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' findings.

claim: Lateral offset of some of the swimmers can passively stabilize the emergent formation in multiple ways.
source: Lastly, we investigated whether lateral offset of some of the swimmers could passively stabilize the emergent formation. The choice of which swimmers to displace laterally and by how much is not unique. Thus, we probed different scenarios and obtained multiple stable formations (Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pairing any two of the four swimmers side-by-side led to cohesive formations.
source: For example, pairing any two of the four swimmers side-by-side, say at the leading, middle, or trailing end of the school, led to cohesive formations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of hydrodynamic cost or benefit varied depending on the spatial pattern of the school and the individual position within the school.
source: The distribution of hydrodynamic cost or benefit varied depending on the spatial pattern of the school and the individual position within the school.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power savings data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Staggering the swimmers in a zigzag pattern stabilized the school, but did not always allow the trailing swimmer to improve its cost of transport.
source: Staggering the swimmers in a zigzag pattern also stabilized the school, but did not always allow the trailing swimmer to improve its cost of transport.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Staggering the swimmers in a 'diamond' formation stabilized the school and led to the highest savings in cost of transport for the entire school of all the stable formations tested.
source: Staggering the swimmers in a 'diamond' formation stabilized the school and, of all the stable formations we tested, led to the highest savings in cost of transport for the entire school (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power savings data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Diamond formations are both stable and energetically optimal.
source: These results are consistent with existing evidence that diamond formations are both stable (Tsang and Kanso, 2013) and energetically optimal (Weihs, 1973; Dai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is consistent with citations to existing literature.

claim: Unlike individuals in an infinite diamond lattice, individuals in a finite diamond formation do not receive equal energetic benefits.
source: But unlike individuals in an infinite diamond lattice (Weihs, 1973), individuals in a finite diamond formation do not receive equal energetic benefits.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the power savings data shown in Figure 10D and contrasts with the theoretical prediction for infinite lattices.

claim: Although many emergent formations do not globally optimize the savings of the entire school, hydrodynamic interactions within these formations offer individuals numerous opportunities to achieve varying levels of energetic savings.
source: Importantly, these findings imply that, although many emergent formations do not globally optimize the savings of the entire school, hydrodynamic interactions within these formations offer individuals numerous opportunities to achieve varying levels of energetic savings (Marras and Porfiri, 2012), potentially creating competition among school members over advantageous positions in the school.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the authors' findings.

claim: Two side-by-side swimmers flapping inphase save energy compared to solitary swimming and share the hydrodynamic benefits nearly equally.
source: Two side-by-side swimmers flapping inphase save energy, compared to solitary swimming, and share the hydrodynamic benefits nearly equally.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When flapping antiphase, side-by-side swimmers exert extra effort compared to solitary swimming.
source: When flapping antiphase, the side-by-side swimmers exert extra effort compared to solitary swimming, contrary to a common misconception that this configuration saves hydrodynamic energy (Zhang and Lauder, 2023b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cost of transport data shown in Figure 3A and contradicts a hypothesis from Zhang and Lauder, 2023b.

claim: The wake of a solitary leader contains information that unveils opportunities for the emergence of stable and energetically favorable formations in pairs of swimmers.
source: Importantly, we showed that the wake of a solitary leader contains information that unveils opportunities for the emergence of stable and energetically favorable formations in pairs of swimmers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Equilibrium locations and trends in power savings and school cohesion can all be predicted entirely from kinematic considerations of the leader's wake with no consideration of the two-way coupling between the two swimmers.
source: Equilibrium locations and trends in power savings and school cohesion can all be predicted entirely from kinematic considerations of the leader's wake with no consideration of the two-way coupling between the two swimmers (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figure 5.

claim: The non-reciprocal or asymmetric nature of flow coupling in leader-follower configurations opens new avenues for future studies of non-reciprocal flow-coupled oscillators.
source: These results are important because they highlight the non-reciprocal or asymmetric nature of flow coupling in leader-follower configurations, inline or diagonal, at finite Re and open new avenues for future studies of non-reciprocal flow-coupled oscillators.
evidence: This is an implication of the authors' findings.

claim: The analysis provides efficient diagnostics and predictive tools that are equally applicable to computational models and experimental data.
source: Our analysis has practical importance in that it provides efficient diagnostics and predictive tools that are equally applicable to computational models and experimental data and could, therefore, be applied broadly to analyze, predict, and test opportunities for schooling and hydrodynamic benefits in live and robotic fish when flow measurements are available.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical utility of the authors' methods.

claim: At an increasing number of flow-coupled swimmers, side-by-side formations remain robust, but inline formations become unstable beyond a critical number of swimmers.
source: At an increasing number of flow-coupled swimmers, side-by-side formations remain robust, but inline formations become unstable beyond a critical number of swimmers (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The critical number of swimmers beyond which inline formations become unstable depends on the fluid properties and can be predicted by analyzing the wake of the leading group of swimmers.
source: The critical number depends on the fluid properties and can be predicted by analyzing the wake of the leading group of swimmers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Field and laboratory experiments have shown that actual fish schools do not generally conform to highly regularized patterns, and schooling fish dynamically change their position in the school.
source: Field and laboratory experiments (Partridge and Pitcher, 1979; Marras et al., 2015; Ashraf et al., 2017; Lombana and Porfiri, 2022) have shown that actual fish schools do not generally conform to highly regularized patterns, and schooling fish dynamically change their position in the school.
evidence: This is a reference to experimental observations from the literature.

claim: In laboratory experiments that challenged groups of fish to sustain high swimming speeds, the fish rearranged themselves in a side-by-side pattern as the speed increased, presumably to save energy.
source: Importantly, in laboratory experiments that challenged groups of fish to sustain high swimming speeds, the fish rearranged themselves in a side-by-side pattern as the speed increased, much like the pattern in Figure 7B, presumably to save energy (Ashraf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a reference to experimental observations from Ashraf et al., 2017.

claim: When the fish are not challenged by a strong background current to sustain high swimming speeds, they position themselves as they please spatially, without much consideration to equal sharing of hydrodynamic benefits.
source: These empirical observations, together with our findings that side-by-side formations provide the fairest distribution of efforts among school members (Figure 7B and C), offer intriguing interpretations of the results in Ashraf et al., 2017; Lombana and Porfiri, 2022: when the fish are not challenged by a strong background current to sustain high swimming speeds, they position themselves as they please spatially, without much consideration to equal sharing of hydrodynamic benefits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations based on the authors' findings.

claim: There is a connection between the resources that arise from flow physics and greedy versus cooperative group behavior.
source: To expand on this, our results suggest a connection between flow physics and what is traditionally thought of as social traits: greed versus cooperation. We posit that there is a connection between the resources that arise from flow physics – in the form of energetic content of the wake of other swimmers – and greedy versus cooperative group behavior.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: In cohesive inline formations, the leader is always disadvantaged and hydrodynamic benefits are accorded entirely to trailing swimmers.

claim: Inline formations could be called greedy, leaving no resources in the environment for trailing swimmers.

claim: Cooperation to achieve an egalitarian distribution of hydrodynamic benefits is forced, not innate.
source: This thought, together with our interpretation of the observations in Ashraf et al., 2017, that cooperation to achieve an egalitarian distribution of hydrodynamic benefits is forced, not innate, raise an interesting hypothesis.

claim: The dynamic repositioning of members within the school could be driven by greed and competition to occupy hydrodynamically advantageous positions.
source: The dynamic repositioning of members within the school (e.g. Figure 10) could be driven by greed and competition to occupy hydrodynamically advantageous positions, much like in peloton of racing cyclists (Blocken et al., 2018).

claim: Flow physics could have acted as a selective pressure in the evolution of social traits such as cooperation and greed in aquatic animal groups.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, it is particularly exciting to explore the prospect that flow physics could have acted as a selective pressure in the evolution of social traits such as cooperation and greed in aquatic animal groups.
